title: Capacity-aware orchestrator for region + tier routing with graceful model variant degradation
creator: Anika Patel
description:
Problem statement:
We need a single decision layer (Policy Orchestrator) that picks region, capacity tier (dedicated vs hosted), and fallback model variants for every incoming request. Current behaviour is router-driven and ad-hoc: when dedicated capacity is saturated we allow immediate spill to hosted with no per-customer safeguards, leading to cost spikes and unpredictable tail-latency. We also lack a standardized, auditable policy for selecting lower-cost / lower-precision model variants when SLOs are at risk.

Goals:
- Make routing decisions capacity- and cost-aware while respecting region/data-residency constraints.
- Prioritize dedicated capacity when customer SLAs require it, but provide safe, rate-limited hosted spillover with per-customer budgets.
- Provide tier- and model-variant fallback rules (e.g., full -> quantized -> distilled) as SLO-preserving, cost-aware degradation paths.
- Ensure decisions are observable, auditable, and reversible (canary/rollout controls).

High-level design (unique aspects):
1) Policy Orchestrator microservice: centralizes routing policies and returns a routing decision object: {priority_tier, region, model_variant, enforcement_flags, telemetry_tags}. This service exposes a small REST/gRPC decision API used by the Router; decisions include soft vs hard routing (soft = recommend but Router can override for emergency).
2) Capacity model + booking: maintain a lightweight capacity model (per-region, per-tier) derived from real-time pool metrics (queued requests, GPU util, reserved commit). Policy Orchestrator can create temporary capacity reservations for high-priority sessions and track per-customer spill budgets.
3) Spillover safeguards (novel): when dedicated pools are above soft thresholds we do not automatically spill all traffic. Instead we apply a per-customer spill budget (tokens per minute/month) and a dynamic admission controller that enforces: i) token budget; ii) request-level cost cap; iii) rate limit multiplier based on recent error/tail-latency.
4) Model-variant degradation ladder (structured): define an ordered list of compatible variants for each canonical model: [full_fp16, int8_quant, distilled_fp16, small-encoder]. Fallback triggers are thresholded metrics: tail latency p95/p99, model queue depth, request error rate, or explicit customer budget exhaustion. The orchestrator selects the first available variant that meets both latency and quality SLO predicates.
5) Region selection rules: combine latency SLOs, data-residency labels, and capacity signal. Prefer same-region dedicated pools; fall back to nearest-region hosted pools only if residency policy allows and cost/latency budgets permit.
6) Circuit breakers and cooling windows: when a model variant begins to degrade (errors or latency spikes) its circuit opens for a cooling window and the orchestrator excludes it for affected customers. A short, progressive probing flow attempts variant reintroduction.
7) Observability & audit: every decision is logged as structured events (decision_id, inputs, reason_codes). Dashboards and an event-driven stream support post-mortem and SLO accounting.

Trade-offs considered:
- Centralized policy vs distributed heuristics: centralization gives consistency and observability but adds a dependency. To mitigate, the Orchestrator can run as a highly-available service with a lightweight local cache in the Router and graceful degradation to last-known-policy.
- Complexity in per-customer budgets: fine-grained budgets prevent runaway costs but increase state. We'll start with a small default budget model and opt into per-customer budgets for committed customers.
- Quality vs cost: fallback to smaller models reduces cost but may regress output fidelity. We'll tie variant selection to quality monitors and provide an opt-out for customers that require deterministic output.

Acceptance criteria / success metrics:
- Router uses Orchestrator decisions for >= 90% of routed requests in the canary cohort.
- Dedicated spill rate (requests spilled to hosted) reduced by 40% for customers with budgets enabled.
- No customer sees >2x monthly cost delta from spill decisions outside of explicit budget/consent.
- SLO preservation: <1% requests routed to a variant that later fails quality checks in the first 7 days of rollout.

Implementation plan (phased):
- Phase 1 (2 weeks): proto Policy Orchestrator service + decision schema; basic capacity model; Router decision integration toggle & local cache.
- Phase 2 (3 weeks): per-customer spill budget, simple model-variant ladder implementation, telemetry events to Kafka, dashboards.
- Phase 3 (3 weeks): circuit-breakers, progressive probing reintroductions, canary rollout to 10% of customers, runbook updates.
- Phase 4 (2 weeks): opt-in per-customer budgets for committed accounts, audit/stamping for enterprise compliance.

Integration points & artifacts:
